script.opening: "Doctor, I’m worried about Maya — she’s only six but over the last few months she’s started developing little breasts and I’ve noticed some pubic hair, and she seems to have shot up in height. Isn’t she far too young for all this? Is something wrong?"

facts.text: Mother, Claire, on video; Maya (6) is in the room playing, shy.

Breast buds noticed about 5 months ago, both sides, now more obvious. Fine pubic hair over the last 2 months. Grown out of two sizes of school uniform this year — "she’s now the tallest in her class; she used to be in the middle".

No vaginal bleeding or discharge. Not sure about body odour — "maybe a bit". No acne. No headaches, no vomiting, no problems with eyesight, not clumsy. No patches of coffee-coloured skin. No change in behaviour.
No creams, gels or medicines in the house containing hormones that Maya could have touched — Claire doesn’t use HRT or a testosterone gel; partner uses nothing. No medicines for Maya.
Healthy, born at term, no hospital admissions, no head injury. Up to date with jabs. Claire started her periods at 12; Maya’s dad "doesn’t know".
Lives with Mum and Mum’s partner, and a younger brother (3). Year 2 at school; a girl at school commented on her chest at swimming.

Anxious, a bit guarded because Maya can hear. Ask: "Why does it matter if it’s early?" and "So what happens now?". If the doctor speaks to Maya kindly, she shakes her head shyly to questions. Ask for an explanation you can repeat to Maya’s dad.

ice.ideas: "It’s too early. Something must be causing it."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — "I’ve been reading online. I’m scared it’s a tumour." Also worried Maya will be teased and will start periods at primary school.
ice.expectations: "Tests to find out why, and to stop it if it needs stopping."

cues: "She seems to have shot up in height" — growth spurt suggesting true puberty.
"I’m scared it’s a tumour" (if worries explored) — needs an honest, calm answer.
"A girl commented at swimming" — psychosocial impact on Maya.

checkpoints.text: Recognises PRECOCIOUS PUBERTY — secondary sexual characteristics before ~8 in girls (~9 in boys) — and that it warrants assessment and paediatric endocrinology referral

Takes a history and arranges a face-to-face examination (growth plotted on the RCPCH UK-WHO chart, Tanner staging with a parent present and not photographed, BP, fundi, fields, neurology, CNS symptoms, possible exogenous hormone exposure including household testosterone gel (MHRA January 2023), family history)
Understands the CENTRAL (gonadotrophin-dependent, often idiopathic in girls but exclude CNS pathology) vs PERIPHERAL (ovarian/adrenal/CAH/McCune-Albright/exogenous) framework
Recognises benign NORMAL VARIANTS (premature thelarche, premature adrenarche) and that they still warrant assessment to distinguish from progressive precocious puberty

Explains WHY assessment matters (final-height impact from early bone maturation, psychosocial impact, not missing a CNS/hormone-secreting tumour or CAH) and REFERS to paediatric endocrinology (bone age, hormones, imaging as the specialist decides; GnRH analogue treatment where indicated), applying NICE NG12 48-hour referral for new central neurological signs
Addresses the parent’s worry and supports the child, explaining the diagnosis and plan sensitively and age-appropriately
Checks understanding and reassures appropriately while conveying the need for proper assessment

Safety-nets and follows up: paediatric endocrinology referral and what assessment involves, red flags (CNS symptoms; vaginal bleeding without breast development → safeguarding consideration), support for parent/child, and review — recognition + appropriate referral, not watchful reassurance alone

worked.txt: "You’re right to bring her — developing breasts and pubic hair at six is earlier than expected, and it’s called precocious puberty. It needs proper assessment, so I’m glad you came."

"Let me take some history, and then I’d like to see Maya face to face to measure and plot her growth, check the stage of development with you present, and check her eyes, blood pressure and nerves. Any headaches or vision changes? Has she had access to any hormone creams or medicines, or does anyone at home use a testosterone gel? And how’s her height compared to before?"

"There are a few possibilities — sometimes the body’s puberty switch turns on early (often no serious cause in girls, but we check), and sometimes a hormone source elsewhere is responsible. There are also milder patterns, like isolated breast development, which can be harmless — but we assess to be sure."

"It’s worth taking seriously for a few reasons: early puberty can affect her final adult height because the bones mature faster, it can be a lot for a young child emotionally, and rarely there’s an underlying cause we’d want to find and treat."

"I’m referring her to the children’s hormone specialists. They’ll do a bone-age X-ray, some blood tests, and scans if they think they’re needed — I don’t need to do blood tests first, and there are treatments — like a medicine that pauses puberty — if that’s the right thing."
"I know this is worrying — most causes are manageable. Come back sooner if she develops headaches, vision problems or anything that concerns you. We’ll support you both through the assessment."

f.learning: PRECOCIOUS PUBERTY is the onset of secondary sexual characteristics before about age 8 in GIRLS and 9 in BOYS, and warrants assessment and paediatric ENDOCRINOLOGY referral. Take a history (timing/progression, growth, family history, CNS symptoms such as headache/visual change, possible exogenous hormone exposure) including household testosterone gel (MHRA Drug Safety Update January 2023), and examine face to face (height and weight plotted on the RCPCH UK-WHO chart for growth velocity, Tanner staging with a parent present and never photographed, BP, fundi, visual fields, neurology, signs of a cause). Understand the framework: CENTRAL (gonadotrophin-dependent, "true") precocious puberty results from early activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis — commoner in girls and often idiopathic, but CNS pathology (tumour, hydrocephalus) must be excluded, especially in boys or with atypical/neurological features — versus PERIPHERAL (gonadotrophin-independent) precocious puberty from ovarian/adrenal/testicular sources, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, McCune-Albright syndrome, or exogenous hormones. Recognise benign NORMAL VARIANTS — premature thelarche (isolated breast development) and premature adrenarche (isolated pubic/axillary hair, body odour) — which are usually benign but still warrant assessment to distinguish from progressive precocious puberty. Evaluation matters because of the psychosocial impact on a young child and family, the effect on final adult height (early bone maturation/premature epiphyseal fusion can reduce final height), and the need not to miss a serious underlying cause (CNS or hormone-secreting tumour, CAH). Refer to paediatric endocrinology for assessment — bone age, hormone testing (LH/FSH, oestradiol/testosterone, GnRH stimulation), and imaging (pelvic/adrenal imaging as indicated, and brain MRI where the specialist judges it indicated — the Endocrine Society 2026 guideline, international, suggests it need not be routine in girls aged 6–8 without neurological findings) — and treatment where indicated (e.g. GnRH analogues (BNFC) to halt central precocious puberty and preserve height/allow age-appropriate development); primary care’s role is recognition, initial assessment and referral, without delaying for GP blood tests. Support the worried parent and the child throughout. NICE NG12: consider a very urgent referral (within 48 hours) for a child with newly abnormal cerebellar or other central neurological function, with same-day assessment for signs of raised intracranial pressure. Vaginal bleeding without breast development, or signs of harm, need safeguarding consideration (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023).

knowledge.summary: Breast development and pubic hair with a growth spurt in a 6-year-old girl is precocious puberty until proved otherwise. The GP’s job is a focused history and examination, prompt referral to paediatric endocrinology, and clear, calm support for the parent and child.

points.t: Signs of puberty before 8 years in girls or 9 years in boys. The first sign is usually breast development in girls and testicular enlargement in boys. Accelerated growth alongside pubertal signs suggests progressive puberty rather than a benign variant.

Central (gonadotrophin-dependent): early activation of the normal axis, usually idiopathic in girls; CNS causes such as tumours or hydrocephalus are commoner in boys. Peripheral (gonadotrophin-independent): ovarian or adrenal sources, congenital adrenal hyperplasia, McCune-Albright syndrome or exogenous sex hormones. Benign variants: premature thelarche (isolated breast development, no growth spurt) and premature adrenarche (pubic or axillary hair and body odour only). Having both breast development and pubic hair with a growth spurt is not an isolated variant.

Onset and progression, growth, headaches, visual symptoms, vomiting, behaviour change, vaginal bleeding, and exposure to hormone creams or gels in the household (MHRA [3]: accidental transfer of testosterone gel). Plot height and weight on the RCPCH UK-WHO chart [4] with any previous measurements and parental heights. Pubertal staging with a parent present; document it and do not photograph. Check for café-au-lait patches, abdominal masses, blood pressure, fundi, visual fields and neurological signs.

NICE NG12 [1]: consider a very urgent referral (within 48 hours) for a child with newly abnormal cerebellar or other central neurological function. Signs of raised intracranial pressure need same-day assessment. Virilisation in a girl, rapid progression, or vaginal bleeding without breast development also need urgent specialist advice.

Refer every child with suspected precocious puberty to paediatric endocrinology. Specialists arrange bone age, LH, FSH and oestradiol, sometimes a GnRH stimulation test, pelvic ultrasound, and brain MRI where indicated; the Endocrine Society 2026 [2] (international) suggests MRI need not be routine in girls aged 6–8 without neurological findings, which is a specialist decision. Do not delay referral waiting for GP blood tests.

Central precocious puberty that is progressing may be treated with a GnRH analogue (BNFC) to pause puberty, protect adult height and allow age-appropriate development; doses follow the specialist. Early puberty can bring teasing, distress and vulnerability; unexplained vaginal bleeding or signs of harm need safeguarding consideration [5].

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Morgan. Hi Maya. (to mother) What’s been worrying you?

Doctor, I’m worried about Maya. She’s only six but over the last few months she’s started developing little breasts and I’ve noticed some pubic hair, and she seems to have shot up in height. Isn’t she far too young for all this? Is something wrong?
You’re right to bring her in. Those changes are earlier than expected at six, so I’ll ask some questions, examine her with you here, and then explain what happens next.
Which came first, the breasts or the hair, and has it been getting more noticeable month by month?
The breasts first I think, then the hair. It’s definitely more obvious now.
You said she’s shot up. Is she growing out of clothes faster than usual?
Yes, a lot faster.
Has Maya had any headaches, problems with her eyesight, being sick, clumsiness, or changes in her behaviour?
No, nothing like that.
Any bleeding from the vagina, spots, or a stronger body odour?
No bleeding. I’m not sure about the smell.
Does anyone at home use hormone creams, gels or patches, for example testosterone or HRT? Children can pick it up from skin contact.
Not that I know of.
Is Maya on any medicines, and has she had any illnesses or head injuries in the past?
No, she’s always been healthy.
What has been going through your mind about what might be causing this?
I’ve been reading online. I’m scared it’s a tumour.
That’s a very understandable fear, and I’ll come back to it. Maya, has anyone said anything about your body at school?
(Maya shakes her head.) (Mother) She hasn’t mentioned anything.

I’d like to measure and weigh Maya, check her tummy, eyes and nerves, look at her skin, and look briefly at her chest and the pubic area, with you here. Maya, is that okay? (Measures height and weight and plots them; asks about previous measurements in the red book; checks blood pressure, skin for café-au-lait patches, abdomen, fundi, visual fields and neurological examination; assesses pubertal stage with mother present, recording findings without photographs.) I’ve plotted her height and I’ll compare it with the earlier red book measurements for the specialists. She has early breast development and some pubic hair, and her nerve and eye examination is normal.
model.why: Growth plotting, pubertal staging with consent, neuro and skin examination

model.text: This is called precocious puberty, which means puberty starting early. In girls the most common reason is that the body’s puberty switch has simply turned on too soon, without any serious cause. Occasionally there is a cause in the brain or in the hormone glands, and that’s why specialists check carefully. Her nerves and eyes are normal today, which is reassuring.
model.why: Names the condition and addresses tumour fear honestly

model.text: Why does it matter if it’s early?
Three reasons. Early puberty makes the bones mature faster, so she could end up shorter as an adult. It can be hard for a young child emotionally. And we want to be sure there’s no underlying cause.
So what happens now?

I’ll refer her to the children’s hormone specialists. They usually do an X-ray of the hand to check bone age, blood tests, sometimes an ultrasound or a brain scan. If needed there is a treatment that pauses puberty until a more usual age.
model.why: Paediatric endocrinology referral and what to expect

model.text: Please bring her back straight away if she gets headaches, especially in the morning, vomiting, problems with her eyes, clumsiness or any bleeding. Can you tell me what you’ll look out for while we wait?
Headaches, being sick, eyesight, clumsiness or bleeding, and come straight back.
That’s right. I’ll send the referral today and see you both in a few weeks, or sooner if you’re worried. Keep answering Maya’s questions simply and honestly.
model.why: Follow-up and support for the child

social.t: Early development can lead to teasing and distress. Talk with the family about what to tell Maya and, if they wish, the school nurse.
If periods are possible, age-appropriate preparation helps her feel less frightened.

legal.t: Examine the child’s body only with the parent present and the child’s agreement. Document staging; do not photograph intimate areas (GMC).
Vaginal bleeding without breast development, or signs of harm, need safeguarding consideration (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023).

professional.t: Explain that idiopathic central puberty is common in girls without promising there is no cause.
Include the sequence of changes, growth measurements, parental heights if known, examination findings and any hormone exposure.

community.t: Previous height records help calculate growth velocity.
If GnRH analogue treatment starts, practices often administer injections under a shared-care agreement.

pitfalls.intro: This station is failed by false reassurance or by frightening the parent. The marks are for recognising the threshold, examining properly, referring promptly, and explaining calmly.

items.why: Pubertal signs before 8 in a girl, with a growth spurt, need specialist assessment.
Growth acceleration separates progressive puberty from benign variants.
items.fix: Measure, plot and use previous records.

items.why: NICE NG12: new central neurological signs in a child warrant a very urgent (48-hour) referral.
items.fix: Ask about headache, vomiting and vision; examine fundi, fields and neurology.

items.why: Accidental transfer of testosterone or other hormone gels causes early puberty (MHRA DSU January 2023).
items.fix: Ask about hormone products in the household.

items.fail: Leaving the tumour fear unaddressed or feeding it.
items.why: The mother’s fear drives the consultation.
items.fix: Name it and give calibrated information.

items.why: Maya is present and may be anxious or teased.
items.fix: Include her, gain her agreement to examination and explain simply.

Vaginal bleeding without breast development, or signs of harm, need safeguarding consideration (Working Together to Safeguard Children 2023).

professional.t: Explain that idiopathic central puberty is common in girls without promising there is no cause.
Include the sequence of changes, growth measurements, parental heights if known, examination findings and any hormone exposure.

community.t: Previous height records help calculate growth velocity.
If GnRH analogue treatment starts, practices often administer injections under a shared-care agreement.

redFlags: Headache, vomiting, visual disturbance or new neurological signs (NICE NG12: consider 48-hour referral; same day if raised ICP)
Exposure to hormone creams or gels
psychosocial: The child’s understanding and experience at school
Vulnerability of a child who looks older
ice: Idea: she is far too young

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: “This is precocious puberty, meaning puberty has started early. In girls it usually has no serious cause, but it needs a specialist assessment.”
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “The body has a switch in the brain that turns puberty on. In Maya it seems to have switched on a few years early. Specialists will check why, and whether to pause it.”

management.reflectIce: “You were scared about a tumour. In girls that’s uncommon, her nerves and eyes are normal today, and the specialists will check carefully.”
management.psychosocial: Include Maya; explain simply; consider school and emotional impact.
sharedPlan: Plot growth and record pubertal stage
Refer to paediatric endocrinology now; no need to wait for GP bloods
Explain likely tests (bone age, hormones, imaging if indicated) and GnRH analogue treatment (BNFC)
safetyNet: Headaches, vomiting, visual change, clumsiness: return urgently (NICE NG12)
Any vaginal bleeding: contact the practice
Review in a few weeks while awaiting the appointment

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station is failed by false reassurance or by frightening the parent. The marks are for recognising the threshold, examining properly, referring promptly, and explaining calmly.

items.why: Pubertal signs before 8 in a girl, with a growth spurt, need specialist assessment.
Growth acceleration separates progressive puberty from benign variants.
items.fix: Measure, plot and use previous records.

items.why: NICE NG12: new central neurological signs in a child warrant a very urgent (48-hour) referral.
items.fix: Ask about headache, vomiting and vision; examine fundi, fields and neurology.

items.why: Accidental transfer of testosterone or other hormone gels causes early puberty (MHRA DSU January 2023).
items.fix: Ask about hormone products in the household.

items.fail: Leaving the tumour fear unaddressed or feeding it.
items.why: The mother’s fear drives the consultation.
items.fix: Name it and give calibrated information.

items.why: Maya is present and may be anxious or teased.
items.fix: Include her, gain her agreement to examination and explain simply.
